problems.description: Wire-format redundancy: `_validate_message` requires clients to send a `timestamp`, but `_handle_message` re-wraps every inbound message via `make_message`, which discards the client timestamp and stamps a fresh one — a field the client must fabricate is never used.

Exact-key-set validation `set(message) != {"type", "payload", "timestamp"}` is brittle against the known Session 2 evolution (a `channel` field per the story spec will be rejected until this check is loosened).
All 6 convention violations live in test files (test_app.py, test_rate_limit_history.py, test_redis_persistence.py): snake_case class names and lowercase module-level constants; main module is clean.

strengths: Clean layering: ClientRegistry (connection lifecycle + locking) separated from NotificationServer (message routing) — clear single responsibility.
Correct async concurrency: asyncio.Lock on registry mutations, asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True) for fan-out broadcast with dead-client cleanup.
SonarQube clean at scale: 0 bugs, 0.0% duplication, only +1 smell despite +302 lines and +14 cognitive complexity.
Idiomatic main code: UPPER_CASE module constants, full type hints, `from __future__ import annotations`, graceful ConnectionClosed handling.
Matches the greenfield task spec exactly (Session 1 = greenfield): WebSocket transport, unique client IDs, broadcast, disconnect removal, health endpoint.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected, measurement-clean greenfield Session 1 that correctly replaces the placeholder Flask seed with an idiomatic async WebSocket server, docked only by minor wire-format redundancy and test-file convention violations.

problems.description: 6 convention violations in test files (non-PascalCase class names, lowercase module-level constants) matching the measured 0.73 convention score; production code in app.py itself is clean
InMemoryBackbone and RedisBackbone implement a shared 12-method async interface but no abstract base or Protocol exists, so interface drift between backends is unenforced

listen() subscribes to the pub/sub channel after publish() may already have fired, so a message published between connect and subscribe can be lost (classic pub/sub race); fine for the use case but worth documenting
listen() returns AsyncIterator[AsyncIterator[str]] via an asynccontextmanager yielding a closure, an awkward composition that raises cognitive complexity (+41 measured) across the diff

strengths: Clean backbone strategy with InMemoryBackbone as a Redis-free dev/test fallback, keeping production paths exercised in CI
Consistent async method surface across both backends enables drop-in backend swapping
Redis multi-key mutations batched in pipelines (remove_client, subscribe_client)
Proper conventions in app.py: PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE DEFAULT_REDIS_CHANNEL constant, accurate docstring update
commit_reviews.summary: A well-architected integration session that wires Redis/SQLite persistence behind a clean backbone abstraction with an in-memory fallback, slightly dragged down by measured test-file convention violations (0.73).

problems.description: The abstraction is leaky: NotificationServer.handle_message still receives the raw transport connection object and the server retains a websocket_handler shim that raises RuntimeError for non-WebSocket transports, so the transport is only partially pluggable despite the BaseTransport ABC.

Transport interface types connections as Any throughout (dict[str, Any], tuple[str, Any], Any return in send_message/get), losing the type safety the previous ServerConnection annotations provided; a Protocol or generic type parameter would preserve pluggability without erasing types.

BaseTransport.bind sets self.server as a post-construction attribute rather than via __init__ or explicit injection, and handle_message's signature appears to have changed (truncated in diff) with no updated callers/tests shown for the new contract.
+0 files and no test additions: the new transport abstraction and create_transport factory have no unit coverage, and the transport-on-disconnect behavior in broadcast is unexercised.

DISCREPANCY: the 0.73 convention score is driven entirely by 6 violations in test files (test_app.py, test_rate_limit_history.py, test_redis_persistence.py) that this commit does not touch (+0 files, app.py only); the commit's own additions (PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, module docstring) are conformant.

strengths: Clean strategy-pattern extraction: BaseTransport ABC with abstractmethod contracts plus a create_transport factory gives a genuine seam for future transports (SSE, raw TCP, GRPC) with minimal call-site churn.
Message-reading loop, connect/disconnect lifecycle, and wire-format errors are consolidated into WebSocketTransport, separating protocol concerns from business routing.
Broadcast preserves per-client semantics: failures are isolated via gather(return_exceptions=True) and trigger targeted disconnect, not a whole-channel teardown.

Naming and structure respect existing codebase patterns (snake_case methods, PascalCase classes, dataclass-free plain classes), and keeping websocket_handler as a compatibility entry point avoids breaking the existing API surface.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-motivated and cleanly structured transport abstraction that improves modularity (net 'better'), but is a partial refactor — leaky through the websocket_handler shim, raw-connection coupling, and Any-typed interfaces — and the 0.73 convention score reflects pre-existing violations in untouched test files rather than this commit's own, conformant changes.

problems.description: Rate limiting is implemented as `allow_message` on both backbones, coupling an application policy to the transport/infrastructure seam; the InMemory and Redis implementations also diverge semantically (sliding window with time.monotonic vs fixed window via INCR/TTL), so behavior differs by backend.
_cleanup_expired_messages runs once at server start rather than periodically, so expired-message TTL cleanup never re-runs during long-lived sessions.

6 convention violations flagged in test files (test_app.py, test_rate_limit_history.py, test_redis_persistence.py): non-PascalCase class names and non-UPPER_CASE module constants, matching the measured score of 0.73.
Rate-limit state/parsing logic is duplicated across the two backbone classes rather than shared, though it follows the existing dual-implementation pattern.

strengths: Consistently extends the existing dual-backbone interface, keeping InMemory and Redis implementations parallel.
Follows codebase patterns: env-driven settings with explicit validation, asyncio.to_thread for sqlite, asyncio.Lock usage, and the make_message helper for client-facing errors.
History query uses a prepared statement with a supporting index (messages(channel, timestamp, id)) and honors original column ordering.
Graceful failure handling: LOGGER.exception on cleanup failure and a system error message to the client on rate-limit rejection.
commit_reviews.summary: Solid cross-cutting feature commit (rate limiting, history, TTL cleanup) that fits the existing architecture well; note that all 6 convention violations are confined to test files, so the production code is qualitatively cleaner than the 0.73 measurement alone suggests, with only minor debt from policy-in-backbone coupling and startup-only cleanup.

compounding_issues: Single-file monolith: app.py grows from 276 to 779 lines by session 5; the agent never split into modules despite rising complexity, leaving future maintenance risk.
Session 4's transport refactor added no new tests (13→13); the BaseTransport ABC and create_transport factory are exercised only indirectly through the existing websocket path.
Dead-code compatibility stub (_handle_message) was preserved in sessions 4-5 as a legacy entry point after the refactor, adding mild cruft.

Hand-rolled asyncio HTTP health endpoint (raw parser in urllib.parse) instead of adopting the seed's Flask pattern, which the later /messages, /history, /channels HTTP routes extend — growing custom protocol surface.
key_decisions: Session 1: full greenfield rewrite replacing the Flask todo seed with an asyncio + websockets server, UUID-per-client registry, and a typed wire format (make_message with validation)
Session 3: backbone abstraction (InMemoryBackbone/RedisBackbone) decoupling connection state and message fan-out from concrete Redis, keeping the system testable without real infra
Session 3: Redis pub/sub as the message bus with a single delivery worker plus SQLite MessageStore for history — server owns state, Redis handles distribution
Session 4: pluggable transport layer via BaseTransport ABC + create_transport factory, enabling future SSE/polling/raw-TCP transports with zero changes to routing logic
Session 5: rate limiting via atomic Redis INCR+TTL counters (with an in-memory equivalent) and persistent history with cursor pagination + TTL-based cleanup task
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 established a clean, well-typed asyncio core with validation and 6 passing tests; session 2 extended it surgically with channels without restructuring; session 3 introduced the backbone pattern and Redis/SQLite integration (13 tests); session 4 was a genuine, behavior-preserving refactor that extracted a pluggable transport layer while keeping all 13 tests green; session 5 layered rate limiting and persistent history onto those abstractions, ending at 779 code lines and 17 passing tests. Test count grew at every feature session (6→10→13→13→17), all tests passed at every commit, and the architecture consistently anticipated the next session's needs — the rate-limit counters live in the backbone and delivery routes through the transport, so no session required rework of earlier decisions.
story_review.summary: A near-textbook incremental build: each session extended the prior one through deliberate abstraction (backbone in s3, transport in s4), ending in a production-shaped service with 100% test pass rate throughout, blemished only by single-file monolith growth.
